section.title: The Request of James and John, and Bartimaeus
section.sectionRationale: The journey to Jerusalem climaxes. Jesus predicts His death a third time in stark detail, yet James and John ask for the best seats in glory, exposing how far the disciples still are from understanding. Jesus answers with the Gospel's key verse: the Son of Man came to serve and give His life as a ransom for many. Then blind Bartimaeus, who sees by faith what the others miss, calls Jesus Son of David, receives his sight, and follows Him on the road, a fitting close to this section on discipleship.
section.thesis: The Son of Man goes to Jerusalem to give His life as a ransom for many, and greatness in His kingdom is cross-shaped service, so that true sight belongs not to the ambitious disciples but to a blind beggar who calls on the Son of David and follows Him on the road to the cross.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the third Passion prediction; the request of James and John and the ransom saying; and the healing of blind Bartimaeus who follows Jesus on the way.

units.label: The third Passion prediction
units.note: we are going up to Jerusalem

verses.text: As they were going up the road to Jerusalem, Jesus was walking ahead of them. The disciples were amazed, but those who followed were afraid. Again Jesus took the Twelve aside and began to tell them what was going to happen to Him:
“Look, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes. They will condemn Him to death and will deliver Him over to the Gentiles,
who will mock Him and spit on Him and flog Him and kill Him. And after three days He will rise again.”

units.label: The request of James and John
units.note: the Son of Man came to give His life a ransom

verses.text: Then James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came to Jesus and declared, “Teacher, we want You to do for us whatever we ask.”
“What do you want Me to do for you?” He inquired.
They answered, “Grant that one of us may sit at Your right hand and the other at Your left in Your glory.”
“You do not know what you are asking,” Jesus replied. “Can you drink the cup I will drink, or be baptized with the baptism I will undergo?”
“We can,” the brothers answered. “You will drink the cup that I drink,” Jesus said, “and you will be baptized with the baptism that I undergo.
But to sit at My right or left is not Mine to grant. These seats belong to those for whom they have been prepared.”
When the ten heard about this, they became indignant with James and John.
So Jesus called them together and said, “You know that those regarded as rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their superiors exercise authority over them.
But it shall not be this way among you. Instead, whoever wants to become great among you must be your {{diakoneo|servant}},
and whoever wants to be first must be the slave of all.
For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a {{lytron|ransom}} for many.”

units.label: Blind Bartimaeus follows on the way
units.note: Son of David, have mercy on me

verses.text: Next, they came to Jericho. And as Jesus and His disciples were leaving Jericho with a large crowd, a blind beggar named Bartimaeus, the son of Timaeus, was sitting beside the road.
When he heard that it was Jesus of Nazareth, he began to cry out, “Jesus, {{huiosdavid|Son of David}}, have mercy on me!”
Many people admonished him to be silent, but he cried out all the louder, “Son of David, have mercy on me!”
Jesus stopped and said, “Call him.” So they called the blind man. “Take courage!” they said. “Get up! He is calling for you.”
Throwing off his cloak, Bartimaeus jumped up and came to Jesus.
“What do you want Me to do for you?” Jesus asked. “{{rabbouni|Rabboni}},” said the blind man, “let me see again.”
“Go,” said Jesus, “your faith has healed you.” And immediately he received his sight and followed Jesus along the road.

diakoneo.gloss: To serve, to wait on, to minister to. Against the world's model of lording it over others, Jesus makes service the measure of greatness in His kingdom, and points to Himself as the servant who serves to the uttermost, giving His life.

lytron.gloss: A ransom, the price paid to release a captive or slave. Jesus interprets His death as a ransom given in the place of many, a substitutionary payment that sets captives free. It is the clearest statement in Mark of why He came to die.

huiosdavid.gloss: Son of David, a title for the promised Messiah of David's royal line. Blind Bartimaeus sees by faith what the sighted crowd misses, hailing Jesus as the messianic King even as He goes up to Jerusalem to reign through the cross.

rabbouni.gloss: My master, my teacher, an intensified and reverent form of Rabbi. Bartimaeus addresses Jesus with heartfelt respect and trust, and his simple request, let me see again, is answered as his faith lays hold of the Son of David.

basic.context: Jesus leads the way up to Jerusalem, and the disciples are amazed and afraid. He tells them plainly, for the third time, that He will be handed over, mocked, flogged, killed, and after three days rise. Astonishingly, James and John respond by asking for the top seats in His glory. Jesus says they do not know what they are asking, and that greatness in His kingdom is not lording it over others but serving, for even He came not to be served but to serve and to give His life as a ransom for many. Then, as they leave Jericho, blind Bartimaeus cries out to Jesus as Son of David, refuses to be silenced, receives his sight, and follows Jesus down the road toward the cross.
basic.hermeneutics: This closes the journey section and its lessons on discipleship. The contrast is deliberate: the disciples who can see grasp for status, while the blind man sees Jesus truly and follows Him. Verse 45 is the theological centre of Mark, explaining the meaning of the death Jesus has repeatedly foretold: a ransom in the place of many. Bartimaeus is the model disciple.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus teaches that the great must diakoneo, serve, and that He came to give His life as a lytron, a ransom, for many. Bartimaeus hails Him as the huiosdavid, the Son of David, and calls Him rabbouni, my master, receiving his sight and following.
basic.typology: The cup Jesus will drink is the cup of God's judgment in the prophets, which He drains for His people. The ransom fulfils the suffering servant of Isaiah 53 who bears the sin of many. The Son of David is the promised messianic King.
basic.christ: Jesus is the servant-King who gives His life as a ransom, the Son of David going up to Jerusalem to reign through the cross, and the One whose true identity a blind beggar confesses when the sighted cannot.
basic.god: God's kingdom runs by the reverse of the world's power. God accomplishes salvation through the self-giving of His Son, a ransom that frees captives, and He opens the eyes of those who cry out in faith.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 53 foretells the servant who bears the sin of many. Psalm 75 speaks of the cup of God's wrath. Isaiah 11 and 2 Samuel 7 promise the Son of David.
basic.oneStory: The road to Jerusalem is the road to the cross, and here Jesus states why He walks it: to give His life as a ransom for many. The disciples still crave glory, but a blind man shows the way, calling on the Son of David and following Him. The whole story now stands at the gates of Jerusalem, where the servant-King will pay the ransom price.

context.literary:
Mark 10:32 to 52 forms the last stretch of the road section that began at 8:22. Two healings of blind men mark its boundaries: the man at Bethsaida who sees in two stages, 8:22 to 26, and Bartimaeus, who sees at once, 10:46 to 52. Between them the disciples are the ones who are slow to see. The word 'way' (hodos) runs through the whole section, from the dispute 'on the way,' 9:33, to the man who follows 'on the way' in 10:52, and it turns the geography into a picture of discipleship.

The third prediction is the longest and most specific. It names who will deliver Him over, what they will do, and the three days. It is also set apart by the opening picture of Jesus walking ahead of a frightened group, 10:32. Then comes the contrast that Mark builds on purpose: after the prediction of 9:31 the disciples argued about who was greatest, and now two of them ask for the highest seats. The pattern of prediction, failure, and correction is the same, but the failure has grown.

The two scenes at the end are linked by a repeated question. In 10:36 Jesus asks James and John, 'What do you want Me to do for you?' In 10:51 He puts the same words to a blind beggar. One asks for glory and receives a warning about a cup. The other asks to see and receives his sight. After this the narrative has no more private teaching on the road. Bartimaeus is the last healing Mark narrates, and he brings Jesus to the gates of Jerusalem with a royal title, which prepares the entry in chapter 11.
context.historical:
The road from Jericho to Jerusalem climbs about a thousand metres in less than twenty miles, and pilgrims coming up to Passover would have been on it in crowds, as the 'large crowd' of 10:46 shows. It is the road on which Jesus walks ahead, which Mark makes a picture of His leadership, since after the resurrection He promises to go ahead of them into Galilee, 14:28 and 16:7. The disciples are 'amazed' and the others 'afraid' because the road leads to the place where, Jesus has said, the leaders will condemn Him.

To sit on the right and left of a king was to hold the highest offices. Solomon had his mother seated at his right hand, 1 Kings 2:19. James and John, with Peter, were the closest of the Twelve, and Matthew adds that their mother made the request, Matthew 20:20 to 21. Mark's account puts their own ambition on display. The 'rulers of the Gentiles' were the client kings and Roman governors the hearers knew, who 'lord it over' their subjects, and Jesus sets His community against that pattern.

A ransom, lytron, was the price paid to free a slave, a captive or a person under obligation, as in Leviticus 25:47 to 49 or Exodus 21:30. Bartimaeus has the title 'son of Timaeus,' which Mark gives in Aramaic and then translates, a detail that may suggest Mark's early readers knew him. Blind beggars sat at roadsides and gates, depending on pilgrims' alms, and the outer cloak he throws off may have been spread out to catch coins, and was in any case his main protection from the cold. Jericho was the city of palms near the Jordan crossing, with Herod's winter palaces nearby. 'Son of David' was a title for the coming king in the Jewish hope; Bartimaeus uses it in a crowd heading to the capital at festival time, and it is the first time in Mark that anyone calls Jesus by it. Jesus does not hush it.
context.canonical:
The saying about the ransom, Mark 10:45, brings together Isaiah 53 and Daniel 7. The Son of Man of Daniel 7:13 to 14 is served by all nations, and Jesus says He came to serve. The servant of Isaiah 53 'bore the sin of many,' 53:12, and 'poured out His life unto death,' and 'the many' of Isaiah is the 'many' of Mark. The same truth is stated by Paul in 1 Timothy 2:5 to 6, where Christ gave Himself as a ransom, and in Titus 2:14 and 1 Peter 1:18 to 19, where the price is His own blood.

The cup comes from the prophets, where it is a figure for the wrath of God, Psalm 75:8, Isaiah 51:17 and Jeremiah 25:15, and Jesus' prayer in Gethsemane, Mark 14:36, shows what He meant in this passage. The kingly language draws on 2 Samuel 7:12 to 13 and Isaiah 11:1, the promise of a descendant of David and a shoot from Jesse's stump.

Bartimaeus's healing belongs with the signs of the new age that Isaiah promised, 'the eyes of the blind will be opened,' Isaiah 35:5, and the servant who would 'open the eyes of the blind,' Isaiah 42:7. After this healing the story moves straight into the entry into Jerusalem. John 13:12 to 15 enacts the teaching on service when Jesus washes His disciples' feet, and Philippians 2:5 to 8 holds it up as the pattern for the church.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Mark wanted his readers to hold together two things that the disciples could not: that the Messiah's path leads through suffering and death, and that His followers must walk the same road. The disciples can hear the plain words, 'they will kill Him,' and then ask for thrones, and Mark lets that contradiction stand so that his readers will recognise their own tendency to listen selectively.

The saying of 10:45 is meant as the key to the whole book. Everything Mark has said about the Son of Man's authority has been about power, and here at last he says what the power is for. Mark's first readers, who may have faced persecution, needed to know that Jesus' death was not an accident or defeat but the purpose of His coming, and that the community He founded was to be known for service.

Bartimaeus is placed last in the section so that the readers end with a person to imitate: one who knows his need, who will not be silenced by the crowd, who leaves what he has, and who follows in the way. Mark invites his hearers to cry out in the same way.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Several parts of the passage are descriptive and unrepeatable. Jesus' death as a ransom is the work only He could do, and the text does not ask believers to pay anything for anyone. The brothers' request and the ten's anger are described, not commended. The cup and baptism that Jesus will undergo are unique to Him, while Jesus says the brothers will share in a different way.

Prescriptive are the lines about leadership, which are given as a rule for the community: it shall not be this way among you. This applies to pastors, parents, employers and all who have influence. The call to cry out to Jesus and follow Him is also an example, since Mark records that Jesus honours it. The healing itself is a one time event. Believers are not promised sight in the same way, but they are promised that He hears those who call and that His kingdom has room for the lowest.

debates.question: What does it mean that Jesus gives His life as a ransom for many?

views.label: A substitutionary payment in the place of many
views.case: The Greek preposition and the ransom image convey Jesus dying in the stead of many, paying the price to free those held captive to sin and death, fulfilling the servant who bears the sin of many in Isaiah 53.

views.label: A liberating price that redefines power
views.case: Set against rulers who lord it over others, the ransom shows a King who reigns by self-giving; His death is the costly act that releases captives and establishes a kingdom of service rather than domination.

debates.bearing: Both readings hold that Jesus' death is purposeful and saving, a costly self-substitution that liberates many and models the servanthood His people are called to.

debates.question: Why does Mark frame this section with the healing of two blind men?

views.label: A parable of spiritual sight
views.case: The bracketing healings mirror the disciples' journey from blindness to sight; Bartimaeus, who sees Jesus as Son of David and follows Him, embodies the clear sight the disciples still lack even as they near Jerusalem.

views.label: A summons to follow on the way
views.case: Bartimaeus followed Jesus along the road, the very road to the cross; his healing becomes a call to true discipleship, seeing Christ rightly and following Him into suffering and glory.

debates.bearing: Both agree Bartimaeus is the model disciple: he sees who Jesus is, calls on Him in faith, and follows Him on the way, in pointed contrast to the status-seeking Twelve.

debates.question: What are the cup and the baptism that Jesus will undergo?

views.label: Suffering and death in general
views.case: Both images describe an overwhelming experience that Jesus must pass through. Luke 12:50 has Jesus speak of a baptism He must undergo and be distressed until it is accomplished. On this reading the brothers are promised that they will share in the suffering that comes to those who follow Him, and James did die by the sword, Acts 12:2.

views.label: The judgment of God borne in the place of others
views.case: In the prophets the cup is the cup of the LORD's wrath, Psalm 75:8, Isaiah 51:17, Jeremiah 25:15. In Gethsemane Jesus prays that the cup might pass from Him, Mark 14:36. On this view the cup is more than martyrdom, since it is the judgment that Jesus alone can drink for others, and the disciples can share only in its consequences, not in its atoning work.

views.label: Both, with different roles
views.case: The brothers' 'We can' is answered with a promise that they will indeed suffer, but the seats are not Jesus' to give. The cup has an aspect only He drinks, and an aspect His followers share, 1 Peter 4:13.

debates.bearing: Whichever shade is stressed, the answer is that glory in this kingdom comes by way of the cup, and that the brothers asked for the crown without knowing what road led to it.

debates.question: Who sits at Jesus' right and left?

views.label: Places reserved by the Father for those He chooses
views.case: Jesus says the seats belong to those for whom they have been prepared, 10:40. He does not name them, and He does not say they will be anyone's merit. He places the decision with the Father, as He does the day and hour in 13:32.

views.label: The two on the crosses
views.case: Mark places two robbers on His right and left at the crucifixion, 15:27. Some readers hear a deliberate irony: the places of glory the brothers sought turn out to be occupied at the cross, which is Jesus' real enthronement. Mark does not say so directly, so the connection is a literary suggestion.

views.label: Seats of humble service
views.case: Jesus quickly turns the question to service, so the real reply is that the greatest place in His kingdom is not an office to be held but a posture. The one who wants to be first is to be the slave of all.

debates.bearing: The text is firm that the seats are not for the asking, and equally firm about the way to them. Readers need not decide who will sit there; they must decide whether they will drink the cup.

study.originalLanguages:
The key saying uses three words worth noticing. The ransom is given 'for many,' anti pollon. The preposition anti means 'in place of' or 'instead of,' and is the standard word for exchange, so the plain sense is substitution. The 'many' is a Semitic idiom, the same as in Isaiah 53:11 to 12, and does not mean 'only some' as against 'all.' It means the multitude that the one stands for, and Paul sets 'the many' beside 'all' in Romans 5:18 to 19 without contradiction. The verb 'to give' (dounai) is joined to 'his life' (psyche), so that the ransom is nothing less than His own life.

The request of the brothers is answered with two images. The 'cup,' poterion, is in the Septuagint the cup of the LORD's wrath, as in Psalm 75:8 and Isaiah 51:17. The 'baptism,' baptisma, comes from the verb to dip or immerse, and here it means to be plunged beneath an overwhelming flood, a sense Luke 12:50 confirms. Both are given in the future and in the language of Jesus' own destiny.

Jesus says rulers 'lord it over' (katakyrieuo) and 'exercise authority' (katexousiazo), both strengthened by the prefix kata, which has the force 'down on' people. Against these He puts diakonos, and then doulos, slave, which is lower. The two words give two steps: servant, who has a duty to others, and slave, who has no claim of his own.

The verbs of the passage keep returning to the opening of the road section. The Son of Man will be 'delivered over,' paradidomi, as in 9:31, and the same word is used in the Septuagint of Isaiah 53:12 of the Servant who was delivered up for their sins. Jesus is walking ahead, proago, and the same verb is used of His going ahead to Galilee, 14:28 and 16:7.

In the story of Bartimaeus, the crowd 'rebuke' him, epitimao, the verb for rebuking demons and storms, to make him be silent, but he 'kept crying out,' the imperfect ekrazen, all the louder. Jesus calls him, and the crowd says, 'Take courage,' tharsei, the same word Jesus used on the lake in 6:50, and 'Get up,' egeire, the verb of rising from the dead. Jesus' question in 10:51 repeats word for word what He said to James and John in 10:36. The man's request, 'let me see again,' anablepo, has the sense of looking up and seeing again. And in 10:52 the verb sozo means both 'heal' and 'save,' the same word as in the disciples' question, 'Who then can be saved?' in 10:26. He followed, imperfect, 'kept following,' en te hodo, on the road.

typology.type: The cup of the LORD's wrath, Psalm 75:8 and Isaiah 51:17
typology.fulfillment: In the prophets the nations and even Jerusalem must drink from the cup of God's fury, drained to the dregs. Jesus takes the image and says He will drink it. The correspondence becomes plain in Gethsemane, where He asks that the cup pass from Him and then submits, Mark 14:36. The escalation is that Isaiah told Jerusalem the cup had been taken from her hand, Isaiah 51:22, and the Gospel shows how: Jesus takes it. Paul says He became a curse for us, Galatians 3:13. The type falls short only in that He drinks it once, not as a repeated punishment, Hebrews 10:12.

typology.type: The Servant who bears the sin of many, Isaiah 53
typology.fulfillment: It was 'the LORD's will to crush Him,' and 'My righteous Servant will justify many, and He will bear their iniquities,' Isaiah 53:10 to 11. Mark's 'ransom for many' echoes the language, and in saying the Son of Man came 'to serve' Jesus draws the picture of the Servant into the title of Daniel 7. The correspondence is of purpose and result: a life poured out and many justified. The escalation is that the Servant of Isaiah is now seen to be the one walking up the road to Jerusalem. The type is still unfolding in that the many are not yet all gathered, Revelation 7:9.

The LORD promised to redeem Israel 'with an outstretched arm' from the yoke of slavery. The word ransom belongs in this world of release, and Jesus' phrase makes His death the price of a greater exodus. The correspondence is that a people held in bondage is freed by an act of God at cost. The escalation is that Jesus redeems from sin and death, Titus 2:14, and the cost is His own life, not a lamb or a firstborn. Luke says Moses and Elijah spoke of His 'departure,' Luke 9:31. The type falls short because Israel's freedom still left them with hearts that turned back, while Christ's work also gives a new heart.

typology.type: Seats at the right and left, 1 Kings 2:19
typology.fulfillment: Solomon placed his mother at his right hand, and the place spoke of honour and nearness to the throne. James and John ask for the same position. The correspondence is of royal court and rank. The escalation is that Jesus' enthronement comes on a cross, where robbers hang at His right and left, Mark 15:27, and then in the glory He foretells before the high priest, 14:62. The type falls short, or is reversed, since the seats the brothers imagined were seats of power and the real ones are seats of suffering.

typology.type: The blind receiving sight, Isaiah 35:5 and 42:7
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah promised that when God came to save, 'the eyes of the blind will be opened,' and the Servant would 'open the eyes of the blind.' Bartimaeus's healing is one of the signs that the promised age has begun. The correspondence is of sign and fulfilment, and the escalation is that physical sight points to the spiritual sight the disciples need. The type falls short because the healing of one man's eyes is a sign and not the whole, and Mark leaves the greater opening of eyes for after the resurrection.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ in the saying that sits at its centre: the Son of Man came to serve and to give His life as a ransom for many. Mark has used the title Son of Man for authority, 2:10 and 2:28, for suffering, 8:31, and for coming glory, 8:38, and 10:45 is the first time it is tied to service and ransom. The one who will come on the clouds, 14:62, is the same One who comes down to the level of a slave, and Paul states the same arc in Philippians 2:6 to 11.

It leads to Christ in what He does with the request. He does not rebuke ambition so much as redirect it: the greatest in His kingdom is the one most like Him. The brothers will drink the cup, which James did when he was put to death, Acts 12:2, and John in exile on Patmos shared in 'the tribulation and kingdom and perseverance that are in Jesus,' Revelation 1:9. Yet the cup in its fullest sense is His alone, and Gethsemane shows what it cost.

It leads to Christ in the title Son of David. The one called by that name by a blind beggar goes up the road to be enthroned, though the throne is a cross. Jesus does not hush the title, as He has silenced others in earlier chapters, and the road is now so near the city that the secret can be set aside. The promise to David of a descendant whose throne would last forever, 2 Samuel 7:12 to 13, is on the verge of being fulfilled in a way no one expected.

It leads to Christ by His compassion for the beggar. He stops, with the crowd and a long march in front of Him, and calls a man the crowd has told to be quiet. The same Jesus who walks ahead to be killed stops for one voice.

A caution is in order. Bartimaeus's cloak is not a coded sign, nor is every detail an allegory of salvation. The links here rest on the passage's own words and on the way later Scripture explains the ransom and the cup.
study.god:
The passage shows a God whose way of exercising power is the opposite of what the nations expect. The rulers of the Gentiles lord it over their people, and the Son of Man, who has every right to be served, gives His life. That says something about the Father's own character, since the Son does not act alone: Jesus says the seats are for those 'for whom they have been prepared,' and the death is purposed and prepared. God is not a distant ruler who requires service; He is the one who serves and gives.

The passage shows God's justice and His mercy together in the idea of ransom. A price is paid, which means that the problem of sin is taken seriously, and the price is paid by God's own Son and not by those who owe it. The cup belongs to the wrath of God, yet the one who drinks it is the Beloved Son. The holiness of God and His love meet here without either being lessened.

It shows God as sovereign over the future. Jesus knows what will happen in detail, delivered, condemned, mocked, spat on, flogged, killed, and risen. Nothing in the coming days will take God by surprise, and the plan will be carried through. The seats at His right and left are in the Father's hand, and no human ambition can reach them.

It shows God as one who hears the cry of the helpless. Bartimaeus cries out, the crowd tries to hush him, and Jesus stops. The God who heard Israel's groaning in Egypt and came down, Exodus 3:7 to 8, is the God who halts a procession for a beggar.

For worship, the passage asks us to bring our requests, as the brothers did, but to be willing to hear the answer, 'You do not know what you are asking.' It asks us to call out as Bartimaeus did, with a plain need and a title for Jesus that is true, and then to follow.

crossReferences.note: The Servant bears the sin of many, pours out His life unto death and justifies many. Mark 10:45 gathers these phrases into a saying of Jesus, so that He presents His own death as the fulfilment of the Servant's work and shows it is no accident but the purpose of His coming.

The cup in the LORD's hand is full of foaming wine, and the wicked drink it to the dregs. When Jesus asks James and John whether they can drink the cup He will drink, He uses an image of divine judgment, which suggests He means something far heavier than a hard life.

Jerusalem is told she has drunk the cup of the LORD's fury to the dregs. Later in the chapter the LORD says He has taken it from her hand, Isaiah 51:22. Jesus' words about the cup are therefore a promise that He will take what others deserved.

In Gethsemane Jesus asks that the cup be taken from Him and yet submits to the Father's will. The scene explains what He meant by the cup in chapter 10 and shows that the question to the brothers was no figure of speech but a description of what was coming.

Matthew's version adds that the mother of the brothers made the request, and then gives the same teaching on service and the ransom. The two accounts together show that the ambition was shared by the family, and that the teaching was given to all the Twelve.

Paul presents Christ, who had every right to equality with God, as one who emptied Himself, took the form of a servant and was obedient to death. The hymn gives the theology behind Jesus' words in 10:45 and shows how the early church read them.

There is one mediator between God and humanity, the man Christ Jesus, who gave Himself as a ransom for all. Paul's wording is close to Mark 10:45 and shows that the church understood the saying as the foundation of the gospel and applied it to all kinds of people.

God promises to redeem Israel from slavery with an outstretched arm. The language of redemption in the Old Testament lies behind the idea of ransom, and Jesus' claim is that a greater deliverance is coming through His death.

When God comes to save, the eyes of the blind will be opened and the lame will leap. Bartimaeus's healing is one of the signs that the promised age has begun, and the title he gives Jesus shows he understood who had come.

God promises David a descendant whose kingdom will last forever. Bartimaeus calls Jesus the Son of David, and the title brings the long promise to the entrance of Jerusalem, where the king will be crowned in an unexpected way.

Jesus washes the disciples' feet and tells them He has set an example. The scene enacts what He taught on the road, that the one who leads is the one who serves, and it shows He asked of them nothing He would not do.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with humans who are made to rule over creation under God and who then try to rule apart from Him. The picture of the Gentile rulers lording it over others is where that story has ended up: power used to dominate. The long story of Israel promises a king from David's line, and the prophets speak of a servant who will bear the sin of many. In Mark 10 these two lines meet: the Son of David is the Servant, and the throne He is walking toward is a cross.

The passage also sets the question that every reader has to answer. The brothers wanted a place in glory and did not know what it cost. Bartimaeus wanted mercy and followed. The story from the garden onward has been about those who grasp and those who receive, and here both are on the same road behind the same Jesus.

The ransom saying looks both back and forward. It looks back to the exodus, in which God bought His people out of slavery at cost, and to the sacrifices that stood in for the guilty. It looks forward to the cross, where the price is paid, and to the people from every nation who are bought, Revelation 5:9. Between those the story passes through the Passover that is just ahead, and Mark has put a blind man at its gate to teach that the door is open to those who cry out.

The end of the story shows that the promise is kept. The Lamb who was slain is worshipped by those He ransomed, Revelation 5:9 to 10, and those who have drunk the cup with Him reign with Him. The one who came to serve will, in the new creation, still be the one who serves, Luke 12:37, and the blind will see, Revelation 22:4: 'they will see His face.' The kingdom the brothers wanted is given, but it is a kingdom of servants, and its King is the one who gave His life.

quiz.q: What did Jesus foretell for the third time as they went up to Jerusalem?

options.text: That the Son of Man would be handed over, mocked, flogged, killed, and after three days rise again.
options.note: Mark 10:33-34 gives the detailed third Passion prediction.

options.text: That He would suffer and die in Jerusalem.
options.note: True but partial; this prediction adds the mocking, flogging, handing to the Gentiles, and rising again.

options.text: That He would enter Jerusalem and be crowned king by the crowds.
options.note: He would be rejected and killed, not crowned by the crowds, though He reigns through the cross.

options.text: That the disciples would be arrested in His place.
options.note: Jesus foretold His own suffering and death, not the disciples' arrest.

quiz.q: How did James and John respond to Jesus' prediction of His death?

options.text: They asked for the seats of highest honour at His right and left in His glory.
options.note: Mark 10:37; they grasped for status even as Jesus spoke of dying.

options.text: They asked to share in whatever Jesus was about to face.
options.note: They claimed they could drink His cup, but their actual request was for glory and honour, not suffering.

options.text: They sought positions of prominence in His coming kingdom.
options.note: Correct in substance, but specifically they asked for the seats at His right and left in glory.

options.text: They offered to die alongside Him.
options.note: They asked for honour, not to die with Him, though Jesus said they would share His cup.

quiz.q: How does Jesus define greatness, and what does He say about His own mission?

options.text: The great must be servants, for the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve and give His life as a ransom for many.
options.note: Mark 10:43-45, the theological heart of the Gospel.

options.text: The great must serve others rather than lord it over them.
options.note: True, but it omits the crucial reason: the Son of Man came to give His life as a ransom.

options.text: The great are those who gain the most authority for good ends.
options.note: Jesus contrasts kingdom greatness with the authority-seeking of worldly rulers.

options.text: Greatness comes from being honoured by others.
options.note: Jesus locates greatness in serving, not in receiving honour.

quiz.q: What does it mean that Jesus gives His life as a ransom for many?

options.text: His death is a substitutionary price paid in the place of many, setting captives free.
options.note: A ransom is a price to free captives; Jesus dies in the stead of many, fulfilling Isaiah 53.

options.text: His death is a costly act that liberates people and redefines power.
options.note: True, but it should include the substitutionary sense of a price paid in the place of many.

options.text: His death is mainly an example of self-sacrifice to inspire us.
options.note: It is an example, but far more: an actual ransom that frees captives, not merely inspiration.

options.text: His death pays a debt owed to the devil.
options.note: Scripture presents the ransom as satisfying God's justice and freeing captives, not a payment to the devil.

quiz.q: How does blind Bartimaeus model true discipleship?

options.text: He sees Jesus by faith as the Son of David, cries out for mercy, receives sight, and follows Him on the road.
options.note: Mark 10:47-52; he grasps Jesus' identity and follows Him toward the cross.

options.text: He persistently asked Jesus for help and was healed.
options.note: True, but it misses his confession of Jesus as Son of David and his following Him on the way.

options.text: He waited quietly until Jesus noticed him.
options.note: The opposite; he cried out all the louder despite being told to be silent.

options.text: He was healed but went home rather than following.
options.note: Mark says he followed Jesus along the road after receiving his sight.

questions: Jesus walked ahead toward the cross while the disciples were amazed and afraid. How does it move you that Jesus went first, resolutely, into suffering for your sake?
James and John sought status even as Jesus spoke of dying. Where do you catch yourself pursuing recognition instead of following the way of the cross?
Jesus said greatness is service. Whom is God calling you to serve this week in a way that costs you something?
Jesus gave His life as a ransom for you. How does dwelling on that price shape your gratitude and your worship?
Bartimaeus threw off his cloak, came to Jesus, and followed Him on the road. What might you need to throw off to follow Jesus more freely?

translationNotes.note: The cup and the baptism are images of the suffering and judgment Jesus will undergo; to drink the cup draws on the Old Testament cup of God's wrath, which He drains in His people's place.

A ransom for many renders lytron anti pollon; the word anti conveys in the place of, marking Jesus' death as a substitution, and many is inclusive, not restrictive, echoing the many of Isaiah 53:11-12.
Rabboni is an Aramaic term of deep respect, my master or my teacher, stronger than Rabbi; Bartimaeus addresses Jesus with trust and reverence.
